claim: The firing of dopaminergic midbrain neurons is thought to reflect prediction errors (PE) that depend on the difference between the value of expected and received rewards.
source: The firing of dopaminergic midbrain neurons is thought to reflect prediction errors (PE) that depend on the difference between the value of expected and received rewards.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Recent work has demonstrated that unexpected changes in value-neutral outcome features, such as identity, can evoke similar responses in dopaminergic neurons.
source: However, recent work has demonstrated that unexpected changes in value-neutral outcome features, such as identity, can evoke similar responses.
evidence: This claim references recent work and is supported by citations in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: Identity PEs were correlated with fMRI activity in midbrain, OFC, piriform cortex, and amygdala.
source: Replicating previous findings, identity PEs were correlated with fMRI activity in midbrain, OFC, piriform cortex, and amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and replicates previous findings.

claim: The magnitude of identity PE responses was independent of the perceptual distance between expected and received outcomes.
source: However, the magnitude of identity PE responses was independent of the perceptual distance between expected and received outcomes, suggesting that identity comparisons underlying sensory PEs may occur in an abstract state space independent of straightforward sensory percepts.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and statistical analyses.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain display firing patterns consistent with prediction errors, which have been taken as a neural substrate of reward learning.
source: Seminal studies have shown that dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain display firing patterns consistent with these errors, which have been taken as a neural substrate of reward learning (Schultz et al., 1997; Schultz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to seminal studies in the field.

claim: Dopaminergic PE responses have been conceptualized to exclusively respond to the difference between the value of expected and received outcomes.
source: Interestingly, unlike the original formulation of PEs as a teaching signal that is agnostic to the type of information that is encoded, dopaminergic PE responses have been conceptualized to exclusively respond to the difference between the value of expected and received outcomes (Glimcher, 2011; Sharpe and Schoenbaum, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Recent work in rats has shown that dopaminergic neurons also respond to violations in the expected identity of outcomes.
source: In contrast to this account, recent work in rats has shown that dopaminergic neurons also respond to violations in the expected identity of outcomes (Takahashi et al., 2017), and that dopamine transients are necessary and sufficient for learning associations between value-neutral stimuli (Chang et al., 2017; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies in rats.

claim: Dopamine transients are necessary and sufficient for learning associations between value-neutral stimuli.
source: In contrast to this account, recent work in rats has shown that dopaminergic neurons also respond to violations in the expected identity of outcomes (Takahashi et al., 2017), and that dopamine transients are necessary and sufficient for learning associations between value-neutral stimuli (Chang et al., 2017; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies have shown similar responses in the midbrain to violations in identity expectations.
source: Human neuroimaging studies have shown similar responses in the midbrain to violations in identity expectations (Boorman et al., 2016; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Identity PEs in the midbrain correlate with updates of outcome identity expectations in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: In addition, identity PEs in the midbrain correlate with updates of outcome identity expectations in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) (Howard and Kahnt, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The magnitude of value-based reward PEs is proportional to the value difference between expected and received outcomes.
source: That is, whereas the magnitude of value-based reward PEs is proportional to the value difference between expected and received outcomes (Abler et al., 2006; Bayer and Glimcher, 2005), a similar modulation of sensory PEs might exist with the value-neutral perceptual distance between expected and received outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on value-based reward PEs.

claim: If identity PEs scale with perceptual distance, outcome expectations are likely to be represented in a space defined by perceptual similarity.
source: If identity PEs scale with perceptual distance, outcome expectations are likely to be represented in a space defined by perceptual similarity (Fontanini and Katz, 2006; Seger and Miller, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothetical claim supported by citations and logical inference.

claim: If identity PEs are independent of perceptual similarity, outcome expectations are more likely to be encoded in an abstract state space involving dimensions other than perceptual similarity.
source: In contrast, if identity PEs are independent of perceptual similarity, this would imply that updates between similar and dissimilar expectations require the same magnitude of change. In turn, this would indicate that outcome expectations are more likely to be encoded in an abstract state space involving dimensions other than perceptual similarity.
evidence: This is a hypothetical claim based on logical inference.

claim: Within an abstract state space, perceptually similar and dissimilar outcomes could be represented with equal distance, allowing for highly specific stimulus-outcome associations even in cases where the perceptual features of different expected outcomes overlap.
source: Within such an abstract state space, perceptually similar and dissimilar outcomes could be represented with equal distance, allowing for highly specific stimulus-outcome associations even in cases where the perceptual features of different expected outcomes overlap.
evidence: This is a hypothetical claim based on logical inference.

claim: There were no significant differences in pleasantness between the four selected odors.
source: Independent ratings confirmed that there were no significant differences in pleasantness between the four selected odors (repeated measures ANOVA, F(3, 54)=1.90, p=0.154; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in pleasantness between the two odor categories (sweet and savory).
source: Likewise, when averaging the two sweet and the two savory odors, there was no significant difference between the two categories (paired t-test, t(18)=1.93, p=0.069).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Within-category odor pairs were significantly more similar than between-category pairs.
source: As expected, similarity ratings confirmed that within-category odor pairs were significantly more similar than between-category pairs (paired t-test, t(18)=6.95, p=1.71×10−6, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Between-category odors were significantly further from each other than within-category odors based on perceptual distances derived from multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) of similarity ratings.
source: Additionally, perceptual distances derived from multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) of similarity ratings showed that between-category odors were significantly further from each other than within-category odors (paired t-test, t(18)=5.67, p=2.21×10−5; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Subjects were able to discriminate between two odors from the same category well above chance (25%).
source: Importantly, despite differences in similarity, subjects were able to discriminate between two odors from the same (one-sample t-test, t(18)=14.35, p=2.70×10−11) and different categories well above chance (25%) (t(18)=33.40, p<0.0001), and there was only a non-significant trend when comparing within- and between-category discriminability (paired t-test, t(18)=−2.07 p=0.053, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Subjects were able to discriminate between two odors from different categories well above chance (25%).
source: Importantly, despite differences in similarity, subjects were able to discriminate between two odors from the same (one-sample t-test, t(18)=14.35, p=2.70×10−11) and different categories well above chance (25%) (t(18)=33.40, p<0.0001), and there was only a non-significant trend when comparing within- and between-category discriminability (paired t-test, t(18)=−2.07 p=0.053, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was only a non-significant trend when comparing within- and between-category discriminability.
source: Importantly, despite differences in similarity, subjects were able to discriminate between two odors from the same (one-sample t-test, t(18)=14.35, p=2.70×10−11) and different categories well above chance (25%) (t(18)=33.40, p<0.0001), and there was only a non-significant trend when comparing within- and between-category discriminability (paired t-test, t(18)=−2.07 p=0.053, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Odor stimuli formed a two-category perceptual similarity structure but were highly discriminable even if odors belonged to the same category.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that odor stimuli formed a two-category perceptual similarity structure but were highly discriminable even if odors belonged to the same category.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Subjects correctly predicted the upcoming odor well above chance (25%).
source: In addition, prediction accuracy was significantly above chance (25%) in trials leading up to a reversal trial (one-sample t-test, t(18)=11.28, p=1.36×10−9), dropped to below chance at the reversal (t(18)= −13.15, p=1.13×10−10), and reverted back to pre-reversal levels on the first post-reversal trial, with post-reversal performance remaining significantly above chance (t(18)=9.83, p=1.15×10−8, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Prediction accuracy dropped to below chance at the reversal trial.
source: In addition, prediction accuracy was significantly above chance (25%) in trials leading up to a reversal trial (one-sample t-test, t(18)=11.28, p=1.36×10−9), dropped to below chance at the reversal (t(18)= −13.15, p=1.13×10−10), and reverted back to pre-reversal levels on the first post-reversal trial, with post-reversal performance remaining significantly above chance (t(18)=9.83, p=1.15×10−8, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Prediction accuracy reverted back to pre-reversal levels on the first post-reversal trial.
source: In addition, prediction accuracy was significantly above chance (25%) in trials leading up to a reversal trial (one-sample t-test, t(18)=11.28, p=1.36×10−9), dropped to below chance at the reversal (t(18)= −13.15, p=1.13×10−10), and reverted back to pre-reversal levels on the first post-reversal trial, with post-reversal performance remaining significantly above chance (t(18)=9.83, p=1.15×10−8, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Updating of stimulus-outcome associations was rapid and did not depend on whether the reversal occurred within or between food categories.
source: This demonstrates that updating of stimulus-outcome associations was rapid and did not depend on whether the reversal occurred within or between food categories.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Subjects accurately identified the delivered odor well above chance levels (25%) in pre-reversal, reversal, and post-reversal trials.
source: In addition, subjects accurately identified the delivered odor well above chance levels (25%) in pre-reversal (one-sample t-test, t(18)=13.80, p=5.19×10−11), reversal (t(18)=13.79, p=5.23×10−11), and post-reversal trials (t(18)=13.60, p=6.59×10−11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Identification performance was independent of reversal type and time.
source: Identification performance was also independent of reversal type and time (repeated measures ANOVA, main effect of type, F(1, 18)=0.86 p=0.366; main effect of time, F(6, 108)=1.01, p=0.415; type x time interaction, F(6, 108)=0.50, p=0.732, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant differences in response time for prediction responses on reversal trials, and there was no effect of reversal type on response time.
source: There were no significant differences in RT for prediction responses on reversal trials, and there was no effect of reversal type on RT (main effect of type, F(1, 18)=0.44, p=0.517; main effect of time, F(6, 108)=0.77, p=0.552; type x time interaction, F(6, 108)=0.94, p=0.452).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of time on response time for identification responses.
source: However, we observed a significant main effect of time on RT for identification responses (F(6, 108)=2.81, p=0.034), which appeared to be driven by longer RTs on reversal trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Subjects were slower to correctly identify an unexpected odor, but this effect was comparable for within- and between-category reversals.
source: This suggests that subjects were slower to correctly identify an unexpected odor, but this effect was comparable for within- and between-category reversals.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Sniff amplitude differed significantly between trial types (non-reversal, between-category reversal, and within-category reversal).
source: Sniff amplitude differed significantly between trial types (repeated measures ANOVA: Type: F(2, 32)=4.12 p=0.033).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect of sniff amplitude differences was driven by significant differences between within-category reversals and non-reversal trials.
source: Post-hoc t-tests revealed that the effect was driven by significant differences between within-category reversals and non-reversal trials (t(16)=-3.13, p=0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No difference in sniff amplitude was found between within-category and between-category reversals.
source: No difference was found between within-category and between-category reversals (t(16)=1.80, p=0.091), or between non-reversal trials and between-category reversals (t(16)=-0.63, p=0.535).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant differences in sniff latency between trial types.
source: There were no significant differences between trial types (repeated measures ANOVA: Type: F(2, 32)=0.89 p=0.405).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No significant differences were found between PE responses evoked by between- vs. within-category reversals in the midbrain.
source: No significant differences were found between PE responses evoked by between- vs. within-category reversals in the midbrain (t(18)=-0.08, p=0.937, Figure 4A), posterior OFC (t(18)=0.77, p=0.451, Figure 4B), PC (t(18)=-0.49, p=0.629, (Figure 4C), and amygdala (t(18)=0.35, p=0.730, Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

source: No significant differences were found between PE responses evoked by between- vs. within-category reversals in the midbrain (t(18)=-0.08, p=0.937, Figure 4A), posterior OFC (t(18)=0.77, p=0.451, Figure 4B), PC (t(18)=-0.49, p=0.629, (Figure 4C), and amygdala (t(18)=0.35, p=0.730, Figure 4D).

claim: A whole-brain analysis revealed no differences between PE responses evoked by between- and within-category reversals, even at a liberal threshold of puncorr <0.001.
source: In addition, a whole-brain analysis revealed no differences between PE responses evoked by between- and within-category reversals, even at a liberal threshold of puncorr <0.001 (or at puncorr <0.05 within the midbrain).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The magnitude of identity PE responses was not modulated by the perceptual similarity of the expected and received outcome.
source: Thus, even at very liberal thresholds, the magnitude of identity PE responses was not modulated by the perceptual similarity of the expected and received outcome.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Parameter estimates from the unmodulated identity PE were significantly higher compared to PEs that were modulated by perceptual distance.
source: Within our a priori ROIs, a ROI-by-modulator ANOVA with repeated measures showed that parameter estimates from the unmodulated identity PE were significantly higher (i.e. PEs explained more variance) compared to PEs that were modulated by perceptual distance (main effect of modulator, F(1, 18)=5.87, p=0.026; interaction, F(3, 45)=0.62, p=0.567).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The main effect of modulator was primarily driven by significantly higher parameter estimates for PEs unmodulated by perceptual distance in posterior OFC.
source: Post-hoc paired t-tests showed that the main effect of modulator was primarily driven by significantly higher parameter estimates for PEs unmodulated by perceptual distance in posterior OFC (t(18)=2.36, p=0.03, Figure 5), but no significant differences were found within the midbrain (t(18)=1.58, p=0.194), PC (t(18)=1.96, p=0.065), and amygdala (t(18)=1.86, p=0.08).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: A cluster in the right midbrain showed fMRI activity that was significantly better explained by PEs that were unmodulated by perceptual distance.
source: We found a cluster in the right midbrain in which fMRI activity was significantly better explained by PEs that were unmodulated by perceptual distance (x = 4, y=−22, z=−20, t(18)=3.78, puncorr = 6.82×10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: No midbrain voxels were better explained by PEs modulated by perceptual distance, even at a liberal threshold of puncorr <0.05.
source: No midbrain voxels were better explained by PEs modulated by perceptual distance, even at a liberal threshold of puncorr <0.05.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Error-related midbrain activity reflects identity PEs that do not reflect the perceptual distance between the expected and received odors.
source: These results suggest that error-related midbrain activity reflects identity PEs that do not reflect the perceptual distance between the expected and received odors.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Identity PEs modulated by MDS-based perceptual distance and unmodulated identity PEs were substantially correlated (r = 0.93 ± 0.05).
source: Of note, identity PEs modulated by MDS-based perceptual distance and unmodulated identity PEs were substantially correlated (r = 0.93 ± 0.05), which may explain the lack of strong differences between parameter estimates reported above.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Perceptual distance is unlikely to play a major role for sensory PEs in the midbrain, OFC, piriform cortex, and amygdala.
source: Overall, these findings further suggest that perceptual distance is unlikely to play a major role for sensory PEs in these regions.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Activity of dopamine neurons in the rat correlates with PEs for value-neutral sensory features, such as identity.
source: This view has recently been challenged by reports that activity of dopamine neurons in the rat (Takahashi et al., 2017) and fMRI responses in the human midbrain (Boorman et al., 2016; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2016) correlate with PEs for value-neutral sensory features, such as identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: fMRI responses in the human midbrain correlate with PEs for value-neutral sensory features, such as identity.
source: This view has recently been challenged by reports that activity of dopamine neurons in the rat (Takahashi et al., 2017) and fMRI responses in the human midbrain (Boorman et al., 2016; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2016) correlate with PEs for value-neutral sensory features, such as identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The identity error in the dopaminergic midbrain did not seem to directly reflect the perceptual distances that participants used to discriminate the odor US.
source: Leaving aside confounds and limitations, which we will address below, the identity error in the dopaminergic midbrain did not seem to directly reflect the perceptual distances that participants used to discriminate the odor US.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Error responses were sensitive to mismatches between expected and received outcomes but contained no information about the magnitude of the mismatch.
source: That error responses were sensitive to mismatches between expected and received outcomes but contained no information about the magnitude of the mismatch indicates that the dimensions of this signal do not necessarily correspond to the identifiable dimensions being used to guide behavior in our simple task.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The dimensions of the identity error signal do not necessarily correspond to the identifiable dimensions being used to guide behavior in the task.
source: That error responses were sensitive to mismatches between expected and received outcomes but contained no information about the magnitude of the mismatch indicates that the dimensions of this signal do not necessarily correspond to the identifiable dimensions being used to guide behavior in our simple task.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The dimension of value PEs maps strongly onto subjective preferences and reward magnitude.
source: On its face, this appears very different from the obvious dimension of value PEs, which map strongly onto subjective preferences and reward magnitude (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Glimcher, 2011; Lak et al., 2014; Schultz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: If identity PEs are dimensionless and reflect simply deviations from expectations, then this puts the burden of tracking the magnitude on downstream areas receiving the error signal.
source: If identity PEs are dimensionless and reflect simply deviations from expectations, then this puts the burden of tracking the magnitude on downstream areas receiving the error signal.
evidence: This is a hypothetical claim based on logical inference.

claim: The identity error signal likely contains some information related to the magnitude of the value-neutral PE.

claim: If sensory PEs are linearly modulated by perceptual distance, this modulation is presumably very small.
source: Taken together, while we cannot rule out the possibility that the present null result is due to insufficient power, we are relatively confident that this was not the case here, and that if sensory PEs are linearly modulated by perceptual distance, this modulation is presumably very small.

claim: fMRI is limited in identifying fine-grained coding structures, at least with the conventional analysis approaches employed in this study.

claim: The entire task occurred within one long fMRI run, preventing the use of more sophisticated multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) approaches.
source: To maximize the number of reversals, the entire task occurred within one long fMRI run, preventing us from using more sophisticated multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) approaches, which are capable of identifying distributed codes but require independent training and test data (Barron et al., 2016; Haynes, 2015; Kahnt, 2018).
evidence: This claim describes the study design and its limitations, supported by citations.

claim: Future studies could use MVPA or unit recordings to look beyond error magnitude and attempt to decode the content that may be signaled by different identity errors.

evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: It is possible that the dynamics of the BOLD signal are more complex than a simple 1:1 mapping between firing rate and fMRI amplitude.
source: Finally, it is possible that the dynamics of the BOLD signal are more complex than a simple 1:1 mapping between firing rate and fMRI amplitude (Logothetis, 2008).

claim: Identity errors are not related in a simple fashion to subjective perceptual distance like value errors are to subjective preferences.
source: That is, while the above technical limitations are important to consider, it seems likely that identity errors are not related in a simple fashion to subjective perceptual distance like value errors are to subjective preferences.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data and reasoning presented.

claim: Perception of categories is just a very small part of what is processed about a sensory event.
source: One suggestion is that perception of categories such as those used here is just a very small part of what is processed about a sensory event.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the nature of sensory processing.

claim: The sensory event is part of a larger overall structure or state representation, which consists of other information about the event and its local context.
source: This simple event is part of a larger overall structure or state representation, which consists of other information about the event and its local context, much of which is not assayed by our simple measure.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the nature of sensory processing.

claim: The findings could be taken as evidence that expected and received outcomes are represented and compared in a larger, more abstract state space, much of which is likely orthogonal to perceptual similarity.
source: Thus, our findings could be taken as evidence that expected and received outcomes are represented and compared in a larger, more abstract state space, much of which is likely orthogonal to perceptual similarity.

source: Future work could directly test this hypothesis by manipulating the state space independently from the sensory space, for example using a design in which two different sensory outcomes could signify the same state.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions.

claim: State encoding could incorporate multiplex, high-dimensional representations of expected outcomes and other task-relevant dimensions.
source: Such state encoding could incorporate multiplex, high-dimensional representations of expected outcomes and other task-relevant dimensions.

source: Recent theories propose that the OFC hosts such state representations (Schuck et al., 2016; Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).

claim: Neuronal and fMRI ensemble activity within the OFC represents expectations about value-neutral features of the outcome, such as identity.
source: In line with this, previous work has shown that neuronal and fMRI ensemble activity within the OFC represents expectations about value-neutral features of the outcome, such as identity (Howard et al., 2015; Howard and Kahnt, 2017; Stalnaker et al., 2014; Wikenheiser et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Trial-by-trial changes in dopaminergic error signals are modulated by representations of hidden states in OFC.
source: Moreover, identity PEs in the midbrain correlate with trial-by-trial updates of identity expectations in the OFC (Howard and Kahnt, 2018), and trial-by-trial changes in dopaminergic error signals are modulated by representations of hidden states in OFC (Jo and Mizumori, 2016; Takahashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The current findings extend the idea that the state space in OFC is not necessarily related to the perceptual similarity of expected outcomes.
source: Our current findings extend these ideas by suggesting that this state space is not necessarily related to the perceptual similarity of expected outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data and reasoning presented.

claim: Similarity between states could reflect other task-relevant variables, such as future states or unobservable contextual features.
source: Similarity between states could reflect other task-relevant variables, such as future states or unobservable contextual features (Schuck et al., 2016).

claim: fMRI activity patterns in the OFC can separate different odor identities within perceptual categories just as well as between categories.
source: This idea is in line with findings that fMRI activity patterns in the OFC can separate different odor identities within perceptual categories just as well as between categories (Howard et al., 2016), suggesting that perceptual similarity is not a driving dimension of OFC ensemble activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Perceptual similarity is not a driving dimension of OFC ensemble activity.
source: This idea is in line with findings that fMRI activity patterns in the OFC can separate different odor identities within perceptual categories just as well as between categories (Howard et al., 2016), suggesting that perceptual similarity is not a driving dimension of OFC ensemble activity.

claim: The current findings provide an important replication for value-neutral sensory PEs in midbrain and OFC.
